speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: asked the Minister for Communications and Information (a) whether the Infocomm Media Development Authority (IMDA) is aware of SingPost’s projected revenue as a result of the increase in postage rate for standard regular mails announced on 19 September 2023; (b) if so, what is the projected amount; (c) whether SingPost requires IMDA’s approval before postage rates are increased; and (d) whether the recent decision to increase postage rate for standard regular mails could have been considered earlier.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: asked the Minister for Communications and Information whether IMDA will take into account the profit of S$38.8 million registered by SingPost in FY2022/23 when working with the company to review its decision to increase postal rates.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: In fact, the average consumer sends less than one letter a month.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: This is the first substantive increase in postage since 2014.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: In the 10 years since, the postal landscape has changed dramatically.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: For example, letter mail volumes have dropped by about half.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: As a Public Postal Licensee, SingPost has an obligation to deliver letters to every addressable place in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: It is also a publicly listed company that engages in non-regulated businesses, such as logistics services and properties, locally and overseas.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: While the overall business of SingPost remains profitable in financial year (FY) 2022, more than 90% of these profits were attributable to its logistics business and largely contributed by its overseas investments.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: This is due to the global decline in letter mail, as well as intense competition from logistics companies and e-commerce players growing their own parcel delivery capabilities.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: As a result, per letter delivery costs have risen considerably.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: After the increase, postage rates in Singapore remain comparable to countries like Japan, which is about 78 Singapore cents, and the United States (US), which is about 86 Singapore cents.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: As noted by several analysts, there is no guarantee that the increase in postage rates will improve the financial position of SingPost.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: The boost to revenues may not compensate for the accelerated decline of letter volumes if customers opt for more e-substitution.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: As part of the postage rate increase, SingPost is also expected to invest in transforming its domestic post and parcel business so it remains efficient and provide high-quality service.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Nonetheless, this is a move that could put SingPost on a more sustainable path to fulfil its obligations as a Public Postal Licensee.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I declare that I am working in an investment firm that has a stake in SingPost.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I asked this Parliamentary Question (PQ) based on my residents' concerns and feedback on the issue.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Some of my residents work as property agents or in organisations like charitable organisations, small businesses, and small and medium enterprises (SMEs) that still depend on domestic postage as a primary mode of advertising and marketing.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: They have, therefore, expressed concerns that the postage hike will affect their livelihoods, especially when there are also price hikes in other areas.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: In addition to the 10 stamps that the Ministry will provide to each household to soften the impact of the increased postage rates, would the Ministry consider some form of targeted help for those who will be particularly affected, like those I mentioned earlier?

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: The bulk of the mail and letters, 80% domestic mail are by corporate entities, most of which are larger corporates like banks and financial institutions, but a significant portion is also by SMEs that the Member has mentioned.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: To mitigate this, SingPost will continue to provide appropriate bulk discounts to businesses and provide other customised support for this group of consumers and businesses.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: SingPost will also continue to honour all first and second local stamp purchased before the rate increase.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: So, to give assurance to the Member's residents who are using these stamps, they will be honoured even after the postal rate increase.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Given how large corporations and, more pertinently, the Government, are the primary users of the postal mail, one is left to wonder whether this price hike does not amount to a tax of the Government on itself and, if so, is there actually a more efficient approach to pass through such cost increases?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: My second question has to do with the fact that cross-subsidisation, as the Senior Minister of State knows, occurs in all businesses.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: So, given overall net profits, is this the best time for the hike or would a delay be more optimal?

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Allow me to be clear in the first instance.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: As shared earlier, there is a global decline in mail volumes.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: In Singapore, the decline has been accelerating in the last few years with the advent of digital technologies and, certainly, over the COVID-19 period.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: We are doing a fundamental review on the future of the postal service.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: In doing so, we want to ensure that the postal service is sustainable for Singapore, sustainable for operators and sustainable for consumers.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: This may require us to relook existing assumptions, such as letter delivery standards.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: The second review is by SingPost – I just wanted this to be clear.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: The Government will work closely with SingPost in its review to ensure that it continues to meet its public postal obligations, while safeguarding the interests of the public and postal workers.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: To the Member's first question, there is a technical clarification.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Most of the mail volume in Singapore is not by the Government.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: The Government contributes to a very small proportion of the total mail volume in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: A shareholder of the company will justifiably ask whether this cross-subsidisation is both ways.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: When the business is doing well outside of Singapore, it is expected to support the not-so-profitable businesses in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: But what happens if it is the other way round?

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: What if its businesses in other countries are loss-making?

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Is there an expectation for us to backstop those losses?

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: So, we have to make clear that this is not the regulatory framework which we are operating under.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: To give some context to the Member, SingPost just celebrated its 165 years of service in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: It is a century-old business and a century-old sector, but the changes to its business model have been quite dramatic in recent years with digital technologies and, certainly, mail volume saw a huge decline during the COVID-19 period.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: So, we are reviewing the fundamental assumptions around the postal service for the long haul to make it more sustainable and fairer.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: While I talked about e-substitution, there is important business correspondence that will still require the basic mail service, although volumes are getting smaller and smaller.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Many Singaporeans have shared with me that it is heartwarming to receive a post card from loved ones overseas or even when a child sends a post card to Santa Claus.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: So, there is a need for the postal service.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: But how do we design a system that is fairer and sustainable for the long haul and where there is commercial incentive for the operator to continue to reinvest in infrastructure, in technology, in automation and, importantly, in jobs and the upgrading of its workers?

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: So, that is at the heart of the review that the Government is doing.
